motion: Is consciousness the ontological foundation of reality rather than an emergent property of matter?

lockedRoutes.description: Analytic idealism reduces reality to consciousness, the sole pre-theoretical given, while treating physicality as a perceptual representation of external mental states.
lockedRoutes.successCriteria: Show that this ontology explains conscious experience, an objective structured world, and causal regularity more parsimoniously than an ontology containing nonmental matter.

motionBridge.description: Consciousness is the ontological foundation rather than an emergent product of matter.

centralBridges.description: Consciousness is the sole directly given category and additional nonmental categories require justification.
Physical properties are representations of mind-independent external mental states.
Intrinsic dispositions of external mental states can ground causal and physical regularity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Strong emergence from nonconscious quantities lacks an intelligible explanatory bridge.
Dissociative boundaries distinguish individual minds from the wider field of mentality.

lockedRoutes.description: Neutral monism avoids substance dualism and the hard problem without identifying the unknown underlying reality specifically as consciousness or mentality.
lockedRoutes.successCriteria: Show that idealism adds no warranted explanation of objective structure, representation, boundaries, or causation beyond a neutral monist account.

motionBridge.description: Neutral monism is sufficient, so consciousness need not be declared reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: The underlying monistic reality should remain ontologically neutral where its nature is unknown.
An adequate ontology must explain the objective world's stable structure and regularities.
Consciousness talk can be reframed in terms of representations without positing a separate substance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Idealism must explain the boundary between private and external states rather than merely name it.
Idealism must identify the source of causal organization within its proposed mental substrate.

lockedSections.title: Foundational ontology and explanatory burden
lockedSections.rationale: The opening clash establishes both sides' ontological routes and the principal burden concerning emergence, neutrality, and explanatory structure.

lockedSections.title: External reality as representation
lockedSections.rationale: This exchange tests whether idealism preserves a mind-independent world and whether calling its substrate mental explains anything further.

lockedSections.title: Explanatory economy and the hard problem
lockedSections.rationale: The moves compare idealism's removal of nonmental ontology with the objection that this maneuver may relocate rather than resolve explanation.

lockedSections.title: Boundaries, causation, and physical regularity
lockedSections.rationale: This section bears directly on whether dissociation and intrinsic dispositions can account for organisms, causation, and predictable physical structure.

lockedSections.title: Representational models and experience
lockedSections.rationale: The final selected exchange tests the neutral-monist representational proposal and idealism's claim that experienced models still presuppose mentality.

lockedMoves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
lockedMoves.proposition: Consciousness is the sole pre-theoretical datum, so reduction should begin from consciousness as a type of existence rather than add an inferred substrate.

lockedMoves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
lockedMoves.proposition: Strong emergence of qualitative experience from nonconscious physical quantities is explanatorily empty because no deduction connects physical parameters to experiential qualities.

lockedMoves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
lockedMoves.proposition: Neutral monism accepts the hard problem's force and rejects dualism, but the unknown underlying unity need not be identified as mental.

lockedMoves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
lockedMoves.proposition: Analytic idealism's dissociation analogy does not explain why the world divides and behaves with its observed physical structure.

lockedMoves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
lockedMoves.proposition: Analytic idealism preserves an external, observer-independent world by treating physical perception as representation of external mental states, not as creation by personal minds.

lockedMoves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
lockedMoves.proposition: Calling an inaccessible external substrate mental adds no clear explanation of the representations or the machinery that constructs them.

lockedMoves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
lockedMoves.proposition: Idealism gains explanatory economy by removing the unnecessary nonmental category whose alleged production of mentality creates the hard problem.

lockedMoves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
lockedMoves.proposition: The sharp boundary between accessible internal states and inaccessible external mental states requires explanation rather than assumption.

lockedMoves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
lockedMoves.proposition: Bodily surfaces represent dissociative boundaries, while external mentality's intrinsic dispositions yield repeatable causal effects and preserve physical and chemical regularities.

lockedMoves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
lockedMoves.proposition: A neutral-monist representational account avoids the hard problem by locating experience in a bat's models rather than in a separately assumed physical bat.

lockedMoves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
lockedMoves.proposition: Representational self-models can be delusions, but their experienced existence still requires mentality and therefore does not rescue materialist illusionism.

lockedMoves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
lockedMoves.proposition: If experience attaches to models, consistency suggests that fleeting models throughout predictive hierarchies have something it is like to be them, not only the self-model.
